can-managers-be-in-a-tip-pool.html.text:
Can managers be in a tip pool?

No, never, regardless of whether the employer takes a tip credit. This page walks through the federal rule on its own, separately from the back-of-house/tip-credit question, because the two get treated as one rule constantly and they are not.

The worked example

Servers and bartenders front-of-house, dishwashers back-of-house and correctly left out of the pool, one shift manager wrongly included, with a $5.12 tip credit taken over four weeks:

RoleCategoryIn pool?Eligible?
Servers (6 × 30 hrs/wk)Front-of-houseYesEligible
Bartenders (2 × 25 hrs/wk)Front-of-houseYesEligible
Dishwashers (2 × 35 hrs/wk)Back-of-houseNon/a -- correctly excluded
Shift manager (1 × 40 hrs/wk)Manager/supervisorYesNot eligible

One manager in the pool is the only violation here -- the dishwashers were correctly left out, so this roster passes the back-of-house test and fails only the manager test. Change any figure and the amount changes with it; run your own roster on the calculator to see your own exposure.

Common questions

Can a manager or supervisor be in a tip pool?

No, never, regardless of whether the employer takes a tip credit. The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2018 amended the FLSA (29 U.S.C. 203(m)) to say an employer may not keep tips received by its employees for any purpose, including allowing managers or supervisors to keep any portion of them. That is a flat prohibition, not a version of the older customarily-and-regularly-receive-tips test -- it applies whether or not the employer takes a tip credit, which is the detail the back-of-house rule depends on and this one does not.

Does it matter if the manager also works the floor during a rush?

No. The rule turns on whether the role is classified as a manager or supervisor, not on how many hours that person spends bussing tables, running food, or serving on a busy Saturday. The manager helped on the floor, so it's fine is the single most common way this rule gets broken, because it sounds like the customarily-and-regularly-tipped logic that governs everything else about tip-pool eligibility, and this rule does not use that logic at all.

What does a manager or supervisor in the pool actually cost?

On the worked example below, servers and bartenders correctly pooled, dishwashers correctly excluded, one shift manager wrongly included, a $5.12 tip credit taken, the front-of-house hours actually pooled are 230 a week. Because a tip credit is taken and the pool has a violation, DOL and the courts that have ruled on this treat the tip credit as forfeited for every front-of-house employee it was taken against: $1,177.60 a week, $4,710.40 across four weeks. That number does not depend on how large a share of tips the manager personally took -- the violation alone forfeits the credit.

Is this the same rule as the back-of-house one?

No -- they are two independent tests, and confusing them is what this calculator exists to catch. The manager prohibition is flat: never eligible, tip-credit status irrelevant. The back-of-house rule is conditional: cooks and dishwashers are eligible only when the employer takes no tip credit at all. A pool can pass one test and fail the other, and this page is about the one that never bends.

FOR RESTAURANT & BAR OWNERS RUNNING A MANDATORY TIP POOL

A tip pool has two federal rules, not one.

Managers and supervisors can never receive tip-pool money — that rule does not care whether you take a tip credit. Back-of-house staff can only be pooled if you take no tip credit at all. On the roster loaded below, a shift manager and the dishwashers are both in the pool while a tip credit is taken, which puts $4,710.40 of back wages at risk over four weeks.

Put your own roster and your own wages in. Everything runs in this browser; nothing is uploaded.

This calculator vs. deciding tip-pool eligibility in a staff meeting — the rule a verbal policy is most likely to get backwards.

Can managers be in a tip pool? — the flat 2018 federal prohibition, on its own, and the myth that breaks it most often.

Your tip credit

Unchecked means you pay full minimum wage or more in cash to every tipped role — several states (CA, NV, WA, OR, MT, AK, MN, and others) require this regardless of what you'd prefer.

The federal maximum tip credit is $5.12/hour (full minimum wage $7.25 minus the federal tipped cash wage floor $2.13). This tool ships no wage table — enter what your own pay stubs actually reflect.

One row per role. Category decides eligibility: front-of-house is always eligible, back-of-house only with no tip credit taken, and a manager or supervisor is never eligible. Leave a row's name blank to skip it.

      Common questions

      Can I ever put a manager or shift lead in the tip pool?

      No, never, regardless of whether you take a tip credit. Congress amended the FLSA in 2018 (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2018, amending 29 U.S.C. 203(m)) to say an employer may not keep tips received by its employees for any purpose, including allowing managers or supervisors to keep any portion of them. That rule does not bend for a manager who also waits tables during a rush — if their job is classified as a manager or supervisor, tip-pool money reaching them is a violation on its own, separate from the back-of-house rule below.

      Can dishwashers or cooks be in the tip pool?

      Only if you take no tip credit at all — pay the full minimum wage in cash to your tipped staff. The Department of Labor's 2021 rule (29 CFR 531.54) calls this a nontraditional tip pool, and it is the one case federal law allows back-of-house staff to share in tips. The moment you take a tip credit, the older, narrower rule applies: the pool is limited to employees who customarily and regularly receive tips — front-of-house only.

      What happens if my tip pool does not comply?

      If you take a tip credit and the pool is later found invalid, DOL and the courts that have ruled on this treat the tip credit as forfeited for every front-of-house employee it was taken against, for the whole period the pool ran — not just for the employee wrongly included. On the worked example below, 230 hours a week of front-of-house time at a $5.12 tip credit is $1,177.60 a week, and $4,710.40 across the four weeks entered. That is back wages owed, and liquidated damages can double it.

      What counts as a tip credit?

      The gap between the full minimum wage and the lower cash wage you actually pay a tipped employee, which federal law lets you close with the tips they keep — up to $5.12 an hour under the federal floor. Several states (California, Nevada, Washington, Oregon, Montana, Alaska, Minnesota, and others) do not allow a tip credit at all, so if your state is one of those, the tip credit taken is $0 and back-of-house staff can be pooled regardless of what this calculator's federal-only exposure figure shows. This calculator ships no rate table — enter the tip credit your own pay stubs actually reflect.

      Is any of this uploaded?

      No. There is no account and the page makes no network requests — it runs entirely in your browser. Your roster, wages, and the figures worked out from them are never sent anywhere and never appear in a usage count. The optional counter records only which features were used and the day, stored on your own device, and it switches itself off for browsers sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.

      Can I save this roster or send it to someone else?

      Yes. Your roster is saved to this browser automatically, so it is still here on your next visit. The copy-link button puts the same figures into the page's own address after the #, which is never sent to a server or logged anywhere, so sending it to a manager or bookkeeper uploads nothing.

      Is this legal advice?

      No. It is arithmetic and a rule lookup against the roster you type, using the federal FLSA rule as of the Department of Labor's 2021 final rule. It does not check state law — several states set stricter tip-pooling or tip-credit rules of their own — and it makes no determination about your specific restaurant's classification of any role. Verify every role's classification and every figure against DOL Fact Sheet #15, your state's wage-hour agency, and a qualified employment attorney before you rely on it.

vs-guessing-from-a-staff-meeting.html.text:
Tip pool compliance calculator vs. deciding it in a staff meeting

Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any point-of-sale, payroll, or restaurant-management product. This page compares the free calculator against the most common way tip-pooling eligibility actually gets decided at a small restaurant or bar: out loud, in a shift or staff meeting, with nobody writing the rule down.

Is a staff meeting enough to set tip-pool eligibility?

A staff meeting can settle who wants to be in the pool. It has no way to check that against a federal rule that most owners have never seen written down as two separate tests: managers and supervisors are never eligible, full stop, and back-of-house staff are eligible only when no tip credit is taken. Those two rules get confused for one rule constantly — "the manager helped bus tables, so it's fine" is exactly the sentence a staff meeting produces and the FLSA does not accept.

The worked example

Same roster, run both ways: servers and bartenders front-of-house, dishwashers back-of-house, and a shift manager, with a $5.12 tip credit taken.

Staff meetingThis calculator
Checks the manager against the rule?Only if someone in the room remembers the 2018 amendmentEvery time, automatically
Checks back-of-house against the tip-credit election?Rarely — "everyone splits it" is the defaultEvery time, automatically

Weekly back-wage exposure if the pool is invalidNot computed$1,177.60
Exposure across four weeksNot computed$4,710.40
Leaves a record you can hand a bookkeeperNo — whoever was in the room remembers it differently by next quarterYes — a link that reopens the exact roster

The staff meeting is not wrong to exist — someone still has to decide who is on shift and who gets a cut. What it cannot do on its own is the rule check, because the rule has two independent branches and a room full of people focused on schedules is not where that gets caught.
